excerpt: When you spend months combing through World War II records for a commemorative coffee table book, the names and places eventually begin to blur together. But every so often, a personal account stops you cold. In 2013, as our committee prepared for the 70th anniversary of the Marianas campaign, I came across the narrative of Marion Olds, one of a handful of Navy nurses captured on Guam in January 1942. What followed was a harrowing voyage into the unknown, defined not by military strategy, but by the fragile comfort of comradeship under the watchful eyes of Japanese sentries. This is her story, as I first discovered it amidst the dusty digital archives.
author: HOUSE OF TAGA DESK
bodyText:
In 2013, while serving as chairperson of our media relations committee, we were deep in the work of planning for a major milestone: the 70th anniversary of the battles of Saipan and Tinian. Our main project was a commemorative coffee table book targeted for June 15, 2014. That meant hours spent digging through archives, looking for personal accounts that could give genuine human context to the historical timeline.

That was how I first came across Marion Olds.

On January 10, 1942, Marion and her fellow navy nurses received a simple, sudden order: pack your belongings and prepare to move. No destination was given. Carrying what little they could, they were driven by truck to the docks, where a dark ship waited at the pier. As the shoreline receded, the reality became clear: they were prisoners, bound for an unknown internment camp somewhere across the Pacific.

Boarding took hours under the gaze of Japanese sentries. Marion took one final look back at the hills of Guam before being sent below deck to a cramped, damp cabin. She shared the space with Ruby Hellmers and Ruby's infant daughter, Charline—a harsh shift from the tropical life they had known just days earlier.

The five-day voyage was spent in constant apprehension. Every pulse of the ship's engine brought the quiet fear that American forces might mistake the vessel for an enemy transport. Daily rations consisted of small bowls of rice with a bit of fish. Through it all, Marion found steadying comfort in Ruby's calm composure and quiet optimism.

When the ship finally stopped, they were brought ashore in Japan. Marion’s resolve wavered on the gangplank, but a quick smile from Ruby kept her moving forward. They were taken to drafty wooden barracks in Zentsuji, where winter was severe. Cold air cut straight through the thin walls, and months of poor food left everyone noticeably weakened.

Conditions improved in March with a transfer to Kobe. Provisions were slightly better, the camp was cleaner, and the guards allowed small freedoms within the compound. Later, when the roar of American bombers filled the sky over Kobe, Marion felt a private sense of reassurance—a clear sign that home had not forgotten them.

After long negotiations and weeks of waiting aboard the *Asama Maru*, the ship finally pulled away on June 25, beginning the long journey back to American soil.
title: From Guam to Kobe
